summary: Describes the Eifel detection algorithm, which lets a TCP sender work out after the fact that it started loss recovery unnecessarily, for example after a spurious timeout. It relies on the TCP Timestamps option. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a package is only late, but the sender thinks it is lost and sends it again. This memo gives the sender a way to notice afterward that it worried for nothing, using time stamps on the packets.

questions: how to detect spurious tcp retransmission

subtitle: Use TCP timestamps to tell, after the fact, whether a retransmission was really needed.

tldr.problem: A TCP sender cannot tell whether the first ACK after a retransmit answers the original or the retransmit. It may then wrongly treat delay or reordering as loss, cut its window and resend data needlessly.
tldr.mechanism: With the Timestamps option enabled, the sender stores the timestamp of the retransmit. If the first acceptable ACK echoes a smaller timestamp, that ACK answered an original transmit, so loss recovery was entered unnecessarily.
tldr.outcome: It only detects spurious recovery; response algorithms are left to other documents. It is an Experimental RFC.

today: RFC 3522 is an Experimental RFC and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only detection and leaves the response step as a placeholder.

sections.title: The Retransmission Ambiguity Problem
sections.content:
After a retransmit, a TCP sender cannot tell whether the first acceptable ACK was sent in response to the original transmit or to the retransmit. This is the retransmission ambiguity problem. The Eifel detection algorithm uses the TCP Timestamps option (RFC 1323) to remove the ambiguity, so the sender can detect a posteriori that it entered loss recovery unnecessarily.

The RFC says this matters where loss recovery gets falsely triggered, for example in wide-area wireless networks where handovers, higher priority traffic or a coverage hole cause sudden delay. This document defines only detection. The response part of the original Eifel proposal is defined elsewhere.
sections.eli5: When you get an answer after asking twice, you cannot tell which ask it answers. A time stamp on each ask fixes that.

sections.title: Events That Falsely Trigger Loss Recovery
sections.content:
Three events can falsely trigger a sender's loss recovery and cause a spurious retransmit plus an unnecessary cut of the congestion window and slow start threshold: a spurious timeout, packet reordering and packet duplication.

A spurious timeout is one that would not have happened had the sender waited longer, because delay suddenly rose in the data or ACK path. Reordering or duplication can make three or more duplicate ACKs arrive, triggering a spurious fast retransmit when the duplicate acknowledgement threshold is three.

A spurious timeout is the more severe case. It forces slow start, and ACKs for original transmits then trigger an implicit go-back-N recovery, so outstanding segments are retransmitted unnecessarily.
sections.eli5: Mail that is only slow, or arrives out of order, can fool the sender into thinking it was lost and resending it all.

sections.title: The Detection Algorithm
sections.content:
If Timestamps are enabled, a sender MAY use the algorithm. When loss recovery starts, with a timeout-based or fast retransmit, it takes these steps and MUST NOT restart them during the same recovery:

  1. Set SpuriousRecovery to FALSE.
  2. Set RetransmitTS to the Timestamp Value of the retransmit.
  3. Wait for an acceptable ACK.
  4. If its Timestamp Echo Reply is smaller than RetransmitTS, go on; otherwise stop.
  5. If the ACK carries a DSACK option, stop. Otherwise, if a DSACK was seen earlier on the connection or the ACK does not acknowledge all outstanding data, go on; else stop.
  6. Set SpuriousRecovery to SPUR_TO (1) for a timeout, or to dupacks+1 for a fast retransmit.

The decision is made on the first acceptable ACK. That lets a future response avoid the go-back-N retransmits, and the scheme is fairly robust against ACK loss because a whole window of ACKs carries the smaller timestamp.
sections.eli5: The sender writes down the time on its second try. If the first answer it hears carries an older time, that answer was for the first try, so the second try was not needed.

sections.title: The Lost-ACKs Corner Case
sections.content:
If every ACK is lost, the sender times out even though the segment arrived. That timeout is unavoidable and should not be treated as spurious. The retransmit arrives as a duplicate, and RFC 1323 says the receiver echoes the timestamp of the last in-sequence segment, which is smaller, so the algorithm would wrongly call it spurious.

Step 5 handles this. A DSACK-enabled receiver puts a DSACK on that ACK, and if no data was lost the ACK acknowledges all outstanding data. Either way the algorithm stops. The RFC notes that some receivers echo the duplicate's timestamp instead, in which case the case does not arise.
sections.eli5: If every thank-you note gets lost, resending is the right thing to do. Extra checks keep the sender from wrongly deciding it worried for nothing.

sections.title: Lying Receivers and the Safe Variant
sections.content:
A receiver can forge echoed timestamps so a genuine retransmit looks spurious. The safe variant treats a segment's timestamp as a secret that only a receiver of that segment knows. Step 2 becomes: set RetransmitTS to the timestamp of the original transmit, which needs the sender to store timestamps of all outstanding original transmits. Step 4 becomes: continue only if the echoed timestamp is equal to RetransmitTS.

The cost is higher sensitivity to ACK losses. A receiver might still guess a lost segment's timestamp, especially with coarse clocks, so the RFC suggests fine-grained timestamps or combining them with a nonce as in ECN. The RFC's Security Considerations say the algorithm does not alter existing protocol state and needs changes only at the sender.
sections.eli5: To prove it saw the first package, a receiver must repeat the first package's secret time. A cheater cannot guess it for a package it never got.
